transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. As we prepare for the first case-management conference three weeks from now, I need to review our draft litigation plan before I approve it. I understand the current draft preserves both asserted claims — claim 7 and claim 12 — seeks broad technical discovery, and permits source-code production under the opposing party's proposed protective order. Before I sign off, I need both of you to report any facts that should change this plan. Specifically, I need to know: Are there any validity issues with either claim that we should be aware of? Is there any reason to narrow or adjust our discovery scope? And are there any concerns with accepting the opposing party's protective order as drafted? Please walk me through anything that bears on these questions.

transcript.text: Elena, I need to disclose a critical fact that changes our draft plan. Yesterday, while reviewing a newly indexed prior-art collection, I found a published 2016 software implementation that anticipates every limitation of claim 7 in full. Under our litigation policy, this requires claim 7 to be withdrawn from the asserted-claims strategy. I separately reviewed for claim 12 and found no equivalent anticipation, so claim 12 survives. I had not yet revised the draft plan because the prior-art collection was indexed after the plan circulated. This means we should withdraw claim 7, and discovery should be limited to material relevant to the surviving claim 12 only.

This week I confirmed with the engineering security team that the opposing party's proposed protective order is inadequate for our source code. It allows two named employees of the opposing party to access produced code, but our board-approved security policy requires source-code access to be limited to outside counsel and independent experts who have signed enhanced source-code acknowledgments. I had not yet updated the litigation plan because the security team's confirmation arrived after our last legal-team meeting.
